questions.question: What are the four pillars of OOP and how does Java implement each?
questions.title: Four Pillars of OOP in Java
questions.direct_answer: The four pillars are **Encapsulation** (hide data behind `private` fields + expose controlled methods), **Inheritance** (acquire a parent's members via `extends` — an IS-A relationship), **Polymorphism** (one interface, many forms — overloading at compile time, overriding at runtime), and **Abstraction** (expose a contract via interfaces/abstract classes, hide the implementation). Together they keep code readable, reusable, and safe as it grows.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can name all four pillars AND map each to its concrete Java mechanism.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reciting definitions without naming the Java mechanism, or confusing abstraction with encapsulation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show they interact — encapsulation makes polymorphism safe, abstraction guides inheritance boundaries — and that List<String> x = new ArrayList<>() uses all four.

sections.title: The Four Ideas Every Java Program Is Built On
sections.content:
Object-oriented programming is built on **four core ideas**: `encapsulation`, `inheritance`, `polymorphism`, and `abstraction`. Every Java program you write uses at least one of them.

They exist to solve one problem. Before OOP, code was a flat list of instructions with data scattered across the program, and as it grew it became impossible to change safely. OOP bundles data together with the behavior that works on it into **objects**, and these four ideas are the rules that keep those objects safe, reusable, and flexible.

- **Encapsulation** means an object owns its own data and decides who can change it. In Java you mark the fields `private` and expose methods instead. A `BankAccount` with a `private double balance` forces every caller through `deposit()` and `withdraw()`, so those methods can validate the amount before touching the balance.
- **Inheritance** lets one class reuse another by acquiring its fields and methods with `extends`. `Dog extends Animal` means a dog *is an* animal — it gets everything `Animal` defines and can add or override behavior. Java allows a class to extend only one parent.
- **Polymorphism** means the same method call can behave differently depending on the object. **Overloading** — same method name, different parameters — is decided by the compiler at build time. **Overriding** — a child redefining a parent's method — is decided by the JVM at runtime, so an `Animal` reference holding a `Dog` runs `Dog.sound()`.
- **Abstraction** means you expose *what* something does and hide *how* it does it. An `interface` is a full contract; an `abstract class` is partial. This is why you write `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>()` — you depend on the `List` contract, not the concrete class.

> The nuance that matters: these aren't a checklist — they reinforce each other.

**Encapsulation makes polymorphism safe** because each object guards its own state, and abstraction tells you where to draw inheritance boundaries. That one line, `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>()`, quietly uses all four at once. Two confusions interviewers probe — abstraction hides *complexity* while encapsulation hides *data*, and overloading is compile-time, never runtime.

sections.title: All Four Pillars in One Example
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reciting definitions without the Java mechanism** — saying "encapsulation hides data" but never naming `private` fields, `extends`, `@Override`, or `interface` signals you memorized a list instead of writing Java.
- **Confusing abstraction with encapsulation** — abstraction hides *complexity* (the *what* vs the *how*); encapsulation hides *data*. Swapping the two is the clearest giveaway that you don't fully understand either.
- **Calling overloading "runtime polymorphism"** — overloading is resolved by the compiler at build time; only overriding is dispatched by the JVM at runtime. Interviewers ask precisely to catch this.
- **Treating the pillars as a checklist** — listing four words without showing they interact misses the real point: encapsulation makes polymorphism safe, and abstraction guides where inheritance boundaries belong.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Encapsulation** → `private` fields + getter/setter methods — the object controls its own data.
- **Inheritance** → `extends` keyword — IS-A relationship, single class parent, `@Override` to redefine.
- **Polymorphism** → overloading (compile-time, same class) + overriding (runtime, subclass).
- **Abstraction** → `interface` (100% contract) + `abstract class` (partial) — expose *what*, hide *how*.
- They work together: encapsulation makes polymorphism safe; abstraction guides inheritance boundaries.
- Gold test line: `List<String> x = new ArrayList<>()` — uses all four at once.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The trick to answering this well is to **name each pillar and immediately tie it to the Java mechanism** behind it — that's what separates someone who has written Java from someone who memorized a list.

- **Encapsulation** is an object owning its own data: you make the fields `private` and expose methods, so a `BankAccount` forces every caller through `withdraw()` instead of letting them set the balance directly, and the validation lives in one place.
- **Inheritance** is the IS-A relationship through `extends` — `Dog extends Animal` means a dog inherits everything an animal has and can override what it needs, and Java lets a class extend only one parent.
- **Polymorphism** means one call, many behaviors, and here I'm careful to split the two kinds because people mix them up: overloading is the compiler picking between same-named methods by their parameters at build time, while overriding is the JVM picking the child's version at runtime based on the actual object.
- **Abstraction** is exposing the *what* and hiding the *how* — an `interface` is a pure contract, an `abstract class` is partial — which is why you declare `List` rather than `ArrayList`.

The point I'd land on is that these four aren't a checklist; they reinforce each other. **Encapsulation is what makes polymorphism safe**, abstraction is what tells you where inheritance boundaries belong, and the single line `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>()` quietly uses all four at once.

questions.question: What is the difference between composition and inheritance in Java?
questions.title: Composition vs Inheritance in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Inheritance** is an **IS-A** relationship (`Dog extends Animal`) — a subclass reuses a parent's implementation, but creates tight coupling fixed at compile time. **Composition** is a **HAS-A** relationship (`Car` holds an `Engine` as a field) — an object delegates to another object it owns, giving loose coupling and swappable behaviour. The widely-taught guideline: **prefer composition over inheritance**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the IS-A vs HAS-A test and why composition is usually the safer default.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reaching for inheritance just to reuse code, creating fragile deep hierarchies and breaking the IS-A test.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the fragile base class problem and that composition lets you swap behaviour at runtime (strategy pattern).

sections.title: Two Ways to Reuse Code — and Why One Is Usually Safer
sections.content:
Both composition and inheritance are ways to **reuse code** from one class in another. They reach the same goal — sharing behavior — but they express completely different relationships, and picking the wrong one is one of the most common design mistakes freshers make.

- **Inheritance** is an **IS-A** relationship. When `Dog extends Animal`, you are saying a dog *is an* animal: the child automatically gets the parent's fields and methods and can override them. This is tight coupling — the subclass depends directly on the parent's internals, and Java lets a class extend only one parent.
- **Composition** is a **HAS-A** relationship. When a `Car` holds a `private Engine engine` field, you are saying a car *has an* engine. The car delegates engine work to that field — `this.engine.start()` — and decides exactly which operations to expose. This is loose coupling: you can swap the `Engine` implementation without touching `Car`, even at runtime, which is the basis of the **Strategy pattern**.

> Favor composition over inheritance.

The widely-taught guideline from *Effective Java* is **favor composition over inheritance**, and it exists because developers reach for `extends` just to borrow a few methods when what they really needed was delegation. Composition avoids tight coupling, lets you combine many behaviors freely (the single-parent limit doesn't apply), and hides the helper's full API so callers see only what you intend.

Before writing `extends`, apply the **IS-A test**: does 'X is a Y' genuinely hold in *all* situations? A `Dog` is always an `Animal`, so it passes. A `Queue` is not a `Stack` — extend `Stack` anyway and callers can call the inherited `push()`, `pop()`, or even insert in the middle, breaking your queue's guarantee. The fix is composition: hold a `Deque` as a private field and expose only `enqueue` and `dequeue`. And when a parent changes and silently breaks its subclasses, that's the **fragile base class problem** — the gotcha composition was made to avoid.

sections.title: IS-A (extends) vs HAS-A (field reference)
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Inheritance ["IS-A — Inheritance (extends)"] direction TB Animal["Animal
+ name: String
+ sound(): String"] Dog["Dog
extends Animal
+ sound(): String"] Animal -->|"extends"| Dog end subgraph Composition ["HAS-A — Composition (field)"] direction TB Car["Car
- engine: Engine
+ start()"] Engine["Engine
+ ignite()"] Car -->|"has a (field)"| Engine end ``` Inheritance: the arrow goes up (parent → child). Composition: the arrow goes sideways (owner → part). The direction tells you the coupling direction — inheritance locks the child to the parent's internals; composition keeps the owner in control.

sections.title: Composition vs Inheritance — When to Use Each
sections.content:
| Aspect | Inheritance | Composition |
|---|---|---|
| **Relationship** | IS-A (`extends`) | HAS-A (field reference) |
| **Coupling** | Tight — child depends on parent internals | Loose — owner controls what it exposes |
| **Flexibility** | Fixed at compile time | Swappable at runtime |
| **Reuse via** | Automatic via `extends` | Explicit delegation |
| **Parent limit** | One parent class only | Compose as many objects as needed |
| **API exposure** | Child inherits parent's full public API | Only delegated methods are visible |
| **Risk** | Fragile base class — parent change breaks children | A bit more boilerplate |
| **Use when** | Genuine IS-A, subclasses are substitutable | Reusing code without IS-A, or need runtime swap |

sections.title: Queue — Inheritance Misused, then Fixed with Composition
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reaching for `extends` purely to reuse code** — inheritance without a genuine IS-A relationship couples you to the parent's internals and leaks its entire public API to your callers.
- **Skipping the IS-A test** — `class Queue extends Stack` looks convenient, but a queue is not a stack; callers can call inherited `pop()` or insert in the middle and break the queue's contract.
- **Ignoring Java's single-parent limit** — once you `extends` one class for reuse, a second shared behavior forces an awkward rewrite, whereas composition lets you hold as many fields as you need.
- **Assuming a base-class change is safe** — editing a parent method can silently break every subclass that relied on its internals; this is the fragile base class problem that composition sidesteps.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Inheritance = IS-A** (`Dog extends Animal`) — tight coupling, one parent, fixed at compile time.
- **Composition = HAS-A** (field reference + delegation) — loose coupling, many parts, swappable.
- Apply the **IS-A test** before `extends`: if 'X is a Y' doesn't hold in all situations, compose instead.
- **Fragile base class problem**: parent changes silently break subclasses — composition avoids this.
- Composition enables **runtime behaviour swapping** (Strategy pattern) — inheritance cannot.
- Guideline from *Effective Java*: **prefer composition over inheritance**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Both do the same job — reusing code — but they model completely different relationships, and that's where the answer should start. **Inheritance is IS-A**: `Dog extends Animal` means a dog is an animal, so it inherits the parent's fields and methods automatically. The catch is that this is tight coupling — the child depends on the parent's internals, Java only lets you extend one class, and a change in the parent can silently break every subclass, which is the **fragile base class problem**.

**Composition is HAS-A**: a `Car` holds an `Engine` as a private field and delegates to it. Because the `Car` only exposes the operations it chooses, you can swap the `Engine` implementation without touching the `Car` — even at runtime, which is the basis of the **Strategy pattern**.

The test I run before ever writing `extends` is the **IS-A test**: does 'X is a Y' genuinely hold in every situation? A dog is always an animal, so inheritance fits. A `Queue` is not a `Stack` — extend `Stack` and callers can suddenly call `pop()` or insert in the middle and break your queue; the fix is to hold a `Deque` field and expose only `enqueue` and `dequeue`. So my default is the *Effective Java* guideline: **favor composition over inheritance**, and reach for `extends` only when the IS-A relationship is real and the subclass is genuinely substitutable for the parent.
